adjudication: Biori aṣṭ and short Shina aṣ show loss of the old accented ending with a short surviving stem; Ashret áaṣṭ then fits later unaspirated closed-a lengthening with early accent. Its early contour therefore does not refute inherited final accent. Kalkoti eeṣ requires an independent vowel/umlaut or numeral-paradigm history; its unmarked citation cannot supply tone.
The full numeral áak and reduced article áa have different coda shapes; do not count them as independent etyma or infer zero tone from unmarked äk/ä.

Palula káaṇ versus Biori kaṇ fits late Ashret closed-a lengthening after rṇ simplification. Short Gilgit kon has nasal-environment backing, and Kalkoti/Kundal kān confirm broader segmental correspondences without reliable tone in these records. A reported mobile Gilgit ear paradigm contrasts with Palula fixed accent despite shared old barytonesis, so the inflectional evidence must override the misleading agreement of short citation forms.

Biori kram beside inflected kráama, and Ashret kráam, separate an older open-syllable lengthening layer from later Ashret closed-syllable lengthening. Metathesis moves r into the onset before this comparison. Shina kom/krom and Kalkoti traam share the work sense but have independent r-cluster and nasal-vowel developments. A single citation-form mora table must be supplemented by the Biori paradigm, which is the most diagnostic evidence.

Village ghróom/draám is a genuine counterexample to the simple Palula E→Kalkoti no-High mapping. Hultman Table6p12 explicitly prints draám beside ghróom. A former extra ending, analogical reaccentuation or contact could explain it, but none is independently demonstrated. Palula ghr also fails to predict Low here; do not hide that second issue.

Palula čúur/Biori čáar and Shina cáar/čáar preserve early accent on a long vowel descending from the old accented vā. Loss of the initial syllable and cluster simplification mean modern initial accent is not retention of old first-syllable accent. Kalkoti čoor and Sauji čōr agree segmentally but their older spellings are not tone evidence. The old short-vowel accusative is a separate input possibility.

Palula tróo/Biori trúu and Shina c̣ée have early prominence after contraction, but their different vowel qualities reflect different monophthongization and raising histories. The old entry has independently distinct masculine, neuter and genitive stems; the exact modern source cannot be assumed from the first headword. Kalkoti traa and Kundal trā are unmarked.

Palula dáand/Biori dan and the Biori inflected dáanda show old root prominence with different lengthening environments. Short Shina don is fixed in the documented Kohistani don/dódi paradigm, supporting barytone inheritance even when the citation cannot show mora accent. Kalkoti daan is explicitly among the toneless comparisons in Hultman's tone table, making it stronger evidence than an ordinary unmarked glossary item.

Palula dáaš/Biori daš fits later Ashret closed-a lengthening with early accent, while Shina dáai/dái loses the sibilant and forms a vowel/glide sequence. Both preserve initial prominence at the level of the historical root, but their mora counts are not directly equivalent. Kalkoti deeš has an independent front-vowel history requiring comparison with other numerals.

Palula and Gilgit dúu have early long prominence; Astori du is short. The broad citation dva conceals accented historical case and gender forms. A development involving dvā́ and raising differs from contraction of duvaú, so modern uu alone cannot identify the antecedent. Kalkoti duu, Kundal duī and Sawi dū add segmental evidence but not uniform mora notation.

Palula dáar beside Biori dar supports early accent on newly lengthened a. The reconstructed short input is distinct from independently attested long dvā́ra. Palula darúṛi ‘window’, Shina darú ‘outside’ and adjectival dariino have additional material or grammatical uses; they are not exceptions in one door paradigm. Sawi darḗ may likewise reflect an ending.

Twelve bóoš/baáš differs in High location. It is an independently identifiable teen compound, and the Kalkoti teen series is reaccented toward the -eéš/-aáš element; report it as compound-series remodeling, not an exceptionless simplex rule.

Palula núu and Shina náu/naw retain prominence on the first material of the old numeral after v weakening/coalescence. The western monophthong and Shina unequal-vowel sequence must not be scored as identical mora structures. Kalkoti nam has a separate final-sonorant development and unmarked tone.
Root neer corresponds to Palula neeṛíi with an accented long final vowel, a different derivation from the canal/bamboo simplex. It falls outside the unaccented short-final-vowel apocope class.

Palula páanǰ/Biori panǰ fits later closed-a lengthening with early accent; Shina poš/poi has nasal-environment backing and affricate/sibilant reduction. The old root prominence is compatible, but the short main-Shina citation cannot reveal a long-mora class. Kalkoti paanǰ and Kundal pā̃j add segmental coverage without a tone decision in these sources.

Palula páand/Biori pan and fixed inflection are compatible with old root prominence followed by later Ashret lengthening. Shina pon is short and reflects nasal-environment backing; Sauji phantē has a retained ending. Since the old headword has short accented a followed by long ā but retains root accent, it is a necessary countercontrol to unrestricted attraction to any later long vowel. The irregular paradigm may explain why final ā is not an ordinary lexical long-vowel target.

Palula bhróo/Biori bhrúu and Shina ẓáa/j̣áa show early root accent, compatible with old long-root barytonesis despite strong segmental divergence. Published Palula bhroó variants elsewhere require separate recording, and Sauji brāū́ ‘my brother’ is a possessive form rather than a bare lexical duplicate. The linked Kalkoti dra is from Liljegren 2013 and is unmarked in that particular citation; its exact tone needs the primary source context.

Man míiš/meéš is Hultman’s explicit counterexample. Palula míiš is EARLY (also Strand mʹîš), not miíš. Its competing manuṣya/martya ancestry and remodeled plurals do not independently establish the missing Kalkoti ending. Keep the High source unresolved.

Palula ráat/Strand rʹât beside Biori rat supports early length from a short stage after cluster reduction. Kalkoti raat is explicitly high-level/default in 2013 and explicitly toneless in Hultman 2023, an important case where zero is positively documented. Kundal and Sauji raːt add segmental evidence; their unmarked tokens do not independently establish zero tone.

Gilgit šáyur/Astori šáwur retain first-syllable prominence, while Kohistani/Guresi šéer and Palula šúur/Biori šáar have contracted early-long forms. The common accent locus can survive very different contraction histories, providing an instructive retention class beyond simple CVCa nouns. Unequal-vowel or glide sequences in the fuller Shina forms require manual alignment.

Biori, Shina, Kundal and Sauji sat are short, while Ashret sáat is early-long. This is a strong demonstration that an old short-root oxytone can pass through a short monosyllable and later acquire an early long vowel; its history differs from kālá > kaál with inherited root length. The retained short forms provide independent chronological evidence rather than merely an inferred intermediate.

Palula sáar versus Biori and Gilgit sar preserves initial/root prominence while Ashret alone has a long vowel. The old first vowel was short, and Biori supplies an independent short-stage control. This supports later monosyllabic lengthening with early alignment, complementary to old oxytones such as saptá that reach the same short stage before lengthening.

Palula díi, bare d-, Kalkoti duun and Kundal di represent different renewed cells of a highly irregular verb. Initial reduplication and old finite morphology are largely lost, so the old third-person accent cannot be projected onto all citations. The perfective requires the separate dattá/dita family.

Palula thíi and Gilgit th-/thu belong to a highly reduced do/make/say paradigm, with much of the old causative stem lost. The modern citation vowel or finite ending carries grammatical information and cannot be equated directly with the old accented pā/yā material. Kalkoti thuun is a present cell, requiring alignment with comparable forms rather than a bare consonantal root.

Palula yhíi/Biori yíi accents the citation ending after substantial contraction or stem reduction, whereas Gilgit yayoók is an infinitive and Kundal yɛ an imperative. Their cell differences and come/go semantic organization prevent a direct comparison of old yā́ti with every modern whole word. The linked Kalkoti yuun citation is from Liljegren 2013; Hultman's yùun supplies explicit low-tone evidence associated with lost aspiration, requiring comparison of the same present cell.

Palula bíi is a modern citation ending attached to a heavily reduced motion root; Strand gives consonantal b-. Shina buž-/bož- and Kalkoti buun preserve different present formations, while perfective go words belong to other historical roots. The database's isolated vr and ẓ are comparative phonological fragments, not independent attested lexical outcomes.

Palula and all four Schmidt Shina dialects bíi retain early accent on the inherited long root after intervocalic j and final a disappear. This provides a particularly clean early-accent control because old ī does not undergo the ā-to-oo raising that complicates many western examples. Hultman's Kalkoti bii is explicitly toneless, a meaningful contrast requiring a separate tonal analysis rather than treating its missing acute as missing data.

Palula khóo/Biori khúu has early root prominence and vowel raising, while Shina khoók/khoónu has late accent in infinitival formations. These are systematic morphological differences, not a single opposite inherited contour. Old khāditá is the relevant perfective comparison and Kohistani khy- may be analogical to the drink perfective; that proposal needs its own paradigm evidence.

Strand gʹûm and Kalkoti goo belong to the perfective go stem. Palula bíi is the dictionary's suppletive citation, not a phonological reflex of gatá and must be excluded from direct sound correspondences. A long early perfective vowel implies either contraction/lengthening followed by morphological root accent or a reformed perfective stem; old final-accent apocope alone is insufficient.

Palula maníi ‘say, call, recite’ accents a modern verbal ending and has lost the old tr material if this etymology is correct. Strand instead links the short man- root to manutḗ. The two proposals cannot be counted as separate lexical outcomes, and modern final accent by itself does not decide the competing segmental derivations.

Palula whíi and Strand wh- are reduced downhill/downstream motion stems, while older wahāndu is a participial form and Kalkoti wuun a present. The proposed ava-vah compound supplies a plausible direction and root, but no old accent is independently attested. The forms must be compared within the motion paradigm and against source-specific low-tone evidence if available.

Thirteen tríiš/treéš joins the independently recognizable Kalkoti teen series with final High. This is compound-series reaccentuation; the old first-accented tráyōdaśa is not a transparent unextended monosyllabic input.

Palula wíi is early long, while Shina wói/wei has a diphthongal sequence. Both have lost enough segmental material that the old three-syllable accent cannot be transferred by counting syllables. A contraction and stem-selection analysis is required; final-accent docking alone would predict the wrong Palula mora if it assumed an already long surviving vowel.

Palula ṣáača ‘climb’, ṣóo ‘put on’ and ṣaawóo ‘dress someone, light’ differ in valency and stem formation, matching an old family that independently contains passive, causative and participial stems. Their different accents cannot be reduced to one sound outcome of sájati. The source explicitly discusses retroflex ṣ spreading from prefixed formations, supplying an independent morphological route for the unusual initial consonant.
Wheat ghoóm/goom has a documented low-level contour in 2013, alongside secondary aspiration/metathesis in Palula. It is not an unmarked no-tone observation.
Belly ḍheér/ḍä̀är has the same Palula L versus Kalkoti Low pattern as salt and wheat. Old root-quantity variants prevent identifying its older mora history from the headword alone.

Palula bheéṇ/Strand bhêʹṇ has late ee after contraction and final-vowel loss. Kalkoti bään belongs to the explicitly low-level set in Liljegren 2013. The old feminine formation and multiple medial-loss stages independently distinguish it from a simple long-root noun; neither parent bhága nor bhagín can be assigned as its accent without argument.

Palula bhiíš and Gilgit/Kohistani/Guresi bií have late long-vowel prominence after substantial contraction of an old finally accented numeral. Their agreement is strong, but the old first vowel was short, so the long vowel must be derived from cluster loss or contraction. Kundal bī̌ requires interpretation of its source's contour notation. The linked Kalkoti biš is a segmental citation in Liljegren 2013; tone must be recovered from an explicitly analyzed token or its source context.

Palula šaák has late accent on old long ā, compatible with final accent in śākhyá after loss of the ending. The parent noun śā́khā has a different accent and must not be substituted silently. Liljegren 2013 analyzes Kalkoti šaàk's falling contour as Low on the second mora, whereas Hultman 2023 analyzes šáak as early High. These are partly alternative phonological analyses of a similar falling pattern, not by themselves evidence of a sound change between 2013 and 2023.

Palula haáḍ beside Biori haḍ provides a strong late-new-aa example with h in a closed monosyllable. haṇḍúk/haḍúng and Strand haḍʹung are extended skeleton or bone forms, not the same cell; marrow is a compound. Kalkoti aḍ/aṛ loses initial h and has separate tone evidence to establish. Turner explicitly calls the ásthi connection very doubtful.
Boy phoó/púu has an accented LONG final vowel in Palula; it is not in the short unaccented final-u apocope class.
Song rhoó/róo follows Palula L→Kalkoti H1, while explicitly lacking Low despite rh. These two dimensions must be kept separate.

Salt lhoóṇ/lùun is a Palula L versus Kalkoti Low correspondence. It is compatible with Low obscuring an otherwise expected early High, but that tonal interaction is a hypothesis rather than a recovered stage.

Palula c̣hiír and Strand c̣hîʹr retain old ī and place accent on its second mora after loss of final accented a. This is a clean long-root oxytone apocope example with aspiration retained; aspiration is not needed to create the contrast. Sauji c̣hir lacks a reliable contour and may have reduced quantity.
Meat maas is explicitly said to lack Low despite Palula mhaás. Its unmarked High status remains conservative/unscored; absence of Low alone does not prove a zero-High category.

Shina koó/keé and Palula kôʹ have late long prominence, while Kohistani/Astori koé/koí preserve unequal-vowel sequences. Turner independently identifies compound replacements for the simple interrogative; their contraction supplies extra moraic material and a reason not to derive every modern form from bare ká. Gender and number also affect the outcomes.
Walnut ac̣hoóṛ/c̣hòor also reduces an entire initial syllable. Its Low may interact with aspiration and onset reanalysis, so it is not a simple same-root monosyllable correspondence.

Mother yéei has an unequal-vowel sequence; Hultman explicitly treats final-vowel loss as relevant, but the conservative automated nucleus test excludes it. Include separately as primary-author analysis.

Palula, four Shina dialects, Dras and Brokskat all show initial short-root prominence in kúṭo/khúṭu-type forms where marked. Kalkoti kuṭ loses the final vowel; Liljegren 2013 Table 12 places it in the high-rising/glottalized group. This supports testing final-unaccented-vowel loss as a Kalkoti conditioning factor without needing an independently known Sanskrit accent.
Cow ghaáu has a vowel sequence and cannot be classified as a transparent unaccented short-u ending. Its apparent counterexample to apocope is excluded for this independent structural reason.

Palula ghína and Shina gin- most directly reflect a nasal-present stem rather than the first dictionary headword. Their root accent is assigned in the modern citation/imperative cell; the old finite nasal inflection carried accent on a different morpheme. Kalkoti giin is a perfective form and giy aal/giyaal a further formation; the newer tone-marked gìin is a key aspiration-loss comparison to check separately.

Palula tóoru and Shina táaro/táaru have early long-root prominence before a gender ending, while Kalkoti taár is high-rising/late H after final-vowel loss. The old entry independently supplies both initially accented tā́rakā and suffix-accented tāraká, so choosing the immediate input requires morphological evidence. The modern ending-loss contrast can be tested without resolving every older accent alternative.

Palula tíiṇu and the four Shina tíiṇo/tíiṇu forms have early long root accent before their gender ending, against old final accent. Retention of old long ī while kṣṇ simplifies makes this a strong extension example with little vowel-alignment ambiguity. Kalkoti tiin adds segmental coverage but no reliable tone in the older unmarked source.

Grandfather and grandmother are two lexemes in one expressive kin family. Both independently retain a short gender vowel in Palula and lose it in Kalkoti. Count lexical cells and broad families separately.

Long is short-vowel dhrígu/dríg. Its Kalkoti outcome is Hshort, which belongs to the final-High result of apocope rather than an invented long rising vowel.

Palula dúṛi has initial short-root accent before i, with shortening and loss of aspiration relative to the reconstructed long root. Kalkoti dur/duṛ loses the final vowel. Neither unmarked Kalkoti tokens nor the unaccented reconstruction license a zero-tone or inherited-accent claim.

Palula níindra and Kundal níndr have initial prominence against old final-accented ā, with an extra nasal and new root length in Palula. Shina nir is short and hides its class. The retained Palula final a means simple final-vowel apocope is not an adequate account; an older nominal formation, paradigm leveling or earlier accent pattern is needed. A pre-Vedic hypothesis requires external comparative evidence, not just this mismatch.

Palula púutru and all four Schmidt Shina dialects póoc̣o preserve early root prominence with a surviving final gender vowel. Sanskrit au is one long nucleus, so its accent must not be misread as accent on a second syllable. The Palula tr versus Shina retroflex affricate provides an independent segmental correspondence. Liljegren 2013 Table 12 explicitly assigns Kalkoti pootr to the high-rising, glottalized group, although the linked segmental citation lacks an acute. That source-level classification supplies a real prosodic comparison.

Palula púutri and Shina póoc̣i retain early prominence on the reflex of old au before the feminine ending. The masculine's independently known accent cannot automatically be assigned to unaccented pautrī. Kalkoti peetr contrasts with grandson pootr, supporting a gender-conditioned vowel history before final-vowel loss.

Palula phéepi has early long prominence before the feminine ending, while Strand phʹôpo denotes the aunt's husband and shows a different vowel and masculine ending. These are a useful gender pair, not variants of one aunt form. Kalkoti pheep is explicitly in Liljegren 2013's low-rising glottalized class; its segment-only token is not toneless.

Palula báabu has early aa, Gilgit and Astori baábo late aa, and Kohistani bubáa final aa. This is a real cross-language morphological and mora difference within a nursery kin term. The unaccented expressive input provides no deterministic inherited-accent prediction; kinship declension and vocative reshaping are concrete alternatives to examine. Kalkoti bab is short.

Palula méeši/Strand mʹêši has early long ee before the feminine ending after contraction of a maternal-aunt compound. This should be compared with phéepi ‘paternal aunt’ as a kinship/gender class, not as direct retention of either mātŕ̥ or svásr̥ accent. Kalkoti meeš lacks final i and requires explicit source tone evidence.

Palula méemi ‘mother's mother’ and móomu ‘mother's father’ have early long root prominence with feminine fronting versus masculine oo. The reconstructed feminine -ikā independently motivates the first form but is not literally the masculine input. Kalkoti meem preserves the fronted vowel after final-vowel loss, providing an independent gender-history control.

Palula and all four Shina dialects súuri retain early long-root prominence with final i. Unlike many unaccented reconstructed extensions, the old family independently records initial accent on sū́riya and sū́rya, making this a strong formation-controlled retention example. Kundal sūr/sīr has lost the ending and varies in vowel quality; Sauji surya preserves fuller consonantal material.

Strand dhrîʹsṭo is an explicitly irregular past form with late long root accent; Kalkoti driṣ and Sauji dərṣo are other perfective reflexes. Palula páaša is the suppletive present/citation and not a phonological reflex of dr̥ṣṭá. The old short vocalic r and modern long ī require a separate stem/quantity history, while final o is morphological.

Gilgit duúr is late, compatible with final-accent apocope, whereas Kohistani/Guresi/Astori dúur is early. Palula dhúura retains a final vowel and early root prominence; its adverbial formation may therefore differ. The other Shina dialects remain early even with consonant-final citations, so retained modern endings alone do not explain the whole split. Kalkoti dùúr adds an independent L from aspiration history.

Palula čhína/Biori čhíne has short initial-root prominence in the imperative, while Gilgit čhin- is unaccented as a bound stem. The old entry independently supplies differently formed nasal-present cells, but the reconstructed citation *chindati has no accent. Modern imperative accent must be analyzed morphologically rather than copied from chinátti.

Palula páaša/Biori páaše and Strand pʹâš- are root-accented and compatible with old present prominence after śy reduction and lengthening. Shina paš- is a bare stem and the infinitives have new suffixes. The past belongs to dr̥ṣṭá under 6518; the two roots must not be confused or counted as independently repeated evidence for one sound correspondence.

Palula píla is a root-accented modern citation with added l, while Shina pi- and Kalkoti piluun/píil/pil belong to different cells. The drink perfective provides an independent analogical model for the eat perfective in Kohistani Shina. The old reduplicated present is not a complete input for all these forms.

Gilgit múu~o ‘dead’ is an early-accented participial adjective with a final ending, while Palula máara is the present/imperative citation of ‘die’, not a direct segmental reflex of mr̥tá. The latter enters this family through lexical/paradigmatic linking and must be replaced by actual muṛ- perfective cells for sound-change analysis. Chilas lik/lič ‘died’ may be a suppletive replacement and requires separate justification.

Palula náawu is early while Gilgit naáwo is late on a long vowel before a preserved w and gender ending. Kohistani nóo~, Guresi náa~ and Astori náu~ have early root prominence with different contraction. Gilgit's late aa therefore cannot be attributed to loss of the visible w alone; a historical extended-stem or geminate/glide stage is needed. This is a stringent residual for a cluster-only account of new late vowels.

Liljegren gháanu is early root-accented in the extended big adjective, compatible with open-syllable short-a lengthening. Strand ghâʹnu is late in the same apparent formation. The modern u/ee feminine alternation supports an inflectional formation, but does not remove the source disagreement. Sauji ghaṇyeṛo has extra derivation and cannot be counted as the same stem.
Sheep yíiṛi/eér preserves the short final feminine vowel only in Palula and matches the final-High apocope outcome.
Horse has both an unaccented final u in Palula and initial voiced aspiration. Kalkoti Low plus final High shows the two conditioning dimensions together.

Palula ǰip and Shina jip/jib are short, so citation forms hide their accent class. Palula's mobile ǰip/ǰipí supports survival of old final accent, whereas Kohistani ǰip/ǰíba is fixed in the grammar. This is a real paradigm divergence despite nearly identical citation forms, and a counterexample to automatic inheritance of fixed/mobile classes across the entire group.

Palula iṇc̣ and Gilgit ic̣ are short monosyllables and therefore do not test mora accent. Their i reflects vocalic-r development, and nasalization is secondary. Longer female-bear forms with final accented ī are derivatives of an independently attested feminine formation; they must not be treated as counterexamples to the root-accented masculine noun.
